Allenes are a class of important organic compounds, and their
synthesis has always been of great interest. In this article, we
have developed a cobalt-catalyzed photoredox strategy, provid-
ing an alternative and efficient approach for the synthesis of
1,3-diarylallenes from propargyl alcohols. The reaction utilized
organic amines as a hydrogen source to avoid the use of con-
ventional hydride additives and does not require the addition of
extra N,N-ligands to activate the cobalt catalyst, achieving a mild
reaction condition. As a result, the reaction was able to synthe-

functional group compatibility.
1.Introduction
Allenes, as an important class of organic structures, are found
to be widely present in natural products, drug molecules, and
functional molecules.[1] In addition, due to the presence of
two C═C bonds, allenes are also a class of synthetic scaf-
folds with high synthetic value, which are extensively used in
organic synthesis, including cycloaddition reactions, nucleophilic
and electrophilic addition reactions, cyclization reactions, etc.,
providing convenient synthetic methods for many important
molecules.[2] In the past few decades, in order to achieve effi-
cient synthesis of allenes, synthetic scientists have developed
many strategies for the synthesis of allenes, in which trans-
formation of propargyl alcohol derivatives into allenes is the
most direct method, including transition metal-catalyzed cou-
pling reactions, Lewis acid or Brønsted acid-promoted propar-
gylic substitutions, metal hydride-mediated hydride reduction,
et al.[3] Relatedly, the strategy of catalytic hydride reduction
of propargyl electrophiles has been an established method for
constructing mono- to tri-substituted allenes (Scheme1a). How-
ever, the currently developed catalytic hydride reductions mostly
depend on metal hydride species, which requires the use of
hydride-based reducing agents in the reaction conditions, such
as aluminium[4] or boron hydrides,[5] formates,[6] and silanes.[7]
This can lead to limitations in functional group tolerance and

Recently, Amgoune and co-workers[9] developed a nickel-
catalyzed photoredox strategy, which efficiently achieved the
conversion of propargyl alcohol derivatives to allene compounds
without the need for a hydride additive (Scheme 1b). How-
ever, the reaction required the addition of a N,N-ligand to
promote the occurrence of the reaction. Moreover, the method
they developed was also incompatible with the synthesis of
1,3-diarylallenes. Cobalt, as an earth-abundant metal, has the
advantages of being inexpensive and readily available. Due to
its excellent catalytic activity, it has been widely used in organic
synthesis, particularly in Pauson–Khand reaction, cross-coupling

of nickel metal, cobalt can also undergo SN2 oxidative addition
reactions with propargyl electrophiles, forming Co-allenyl or Co-
propargyl intermediates, thereby facilitating the transformation
of propargyl electrophiles.[11] To the best of our knowledge, the
reduction of propargyl electrophiles catalyzed by cobalt has not
yet been developed. In order to further develop the synthetic
methods of allenes and leverage the catalytic advantages of
metal cobalt, as well as our recent interesting in transformation
of propargyl alcohols.[12] In this paper, we developed a cobalt-
catalyzed reduction strategy for propargyl alcohol derivatives,
achieving the synthesis of 1,3-diarylallenes (Scheme1c). As an
improvement, the reaction did not require hydride additive or
ligands, leading to the mild conditions.

after releasing CO 2.[13] Subsequently, under the action of
the alkyl radical specie B which generated from intermedi-
ate A via a deprotonation process, a single-electron transfer

is finally protonated to produce the allene products 2 and

3.Conclusion
In summary, a method for the photocatalytic reduction of
propargyl alcohols has been successfully developed, capable of
achieving an efficient transformation of a series of propargyl
alcohols into allene compounds, particularly the synthesis of
1,3-diarylallenes. This method has several advantages, including
good yields, good functional group tolerance, the use of the
inexpensive metal cobalt as a catalyst without the need for addi-
tional ligands, the use of organic amines as a hydrogen source
without the need for hydride additives, and the use of non-toxic
solvents. More transformations of propargyl alcohol derivatives
catalyzed by cobalt are under development in our lab.

1,3-diarylallenes. After screening diferent catalysts, we were sur-
prised to find that under Co(acac) condition, substrate 1a could
achieve a 75% yield of the desired product 2a. And it is worth
mentioning that no additional ligand was required in the reac
tion conditions. Moreover, other leaving groups, including OAc,
OBz, etc., could not provide better reaction results. In addition,
when using propargyl alcohol 1e as the substrate directly, the
reaction did not proceed normally. Therefore, we identified the
OBoc group as the optimal leaving group for our subsequent
research.

After determining the most eficient leaving group, we next
investigated and optimized other reaction factors (Table 2).
Firstly, the screening of solvents showed that acetone still
remained the optimal reaction solvent, and this reaction could

not proceed normally under protic solvent conditions. Chang-
ing the cobalt catalyst also failed to further improve the reaction
yield (Table 2, entries 7–10). Next, we systematically examined the
impact of photocatalysts on the reaction, including Ir complexes,
Ru complexes, and organic photocatalysts. It was found that
the photocatalyst PC-3 could significantly improve the reaction,
increasing the yield to 90% (Table 2, entry 15).

After obtaining the optimal reaction conditions, we sys-
tematically investigated the scope of this reaction as shown
in Scheme 2. Under the optimal conditions, the isolated yield
of the template product 2a could reach 91%. The aryl group
(R<sup>1</sup>) connected to the alkyne could tolerate both electron-
withdrawing and electron-donating groups, and the correspond-
ing 1,3-diarylallenes 2b-2i could be synthesized with moderate
to excellent yields. Alkyl propargyl alcohol derivative could also
serve as a suitable substrate, forming the product 2j with a

propargyl alcohol structure and found that the substrate could
not only tolerate other alkyl substituents, including Bn, i-Pr and
cyclohexyl, but also the hydrogen atom. Moreover, we found
that cyclohexyl-substituted propargyl alcohols could synthesize
the corresponding 1,3-diaryl allene products 2n-2r more efi-
ciently, possibly due to the enhanced stability of the products.
For the R<sup>3</sup> substituent, it could not only tolerate diferently sub-
stituted phenyl groups but also naphthyl, thiophene, and others,
with forming the corresponding products 2s-2x in 46%–96%
yield. It is worth mentioning that the reaction could also toler-

ate dialkyl-substituted propargyl alcohol derivatives, ultimately
converting into the corresponding products 2z-2bb with mod-
erate yields. Therefore, our reaction could not only synthesize
1,3-diarylallenes but was also applicable to the synthesis of 1-aryl-
3-alkyl allenes. However, a propargyl alcohol derivative bearing
fully aliphatic substituents could not be converted into the final
products.

To verify the synthetic potential of the reaction, we inves-
tigated the scaled-up reaction. The results showed that the
reaction could be scaled up to the gram level while maintaining
consistent reaction eficiency (Scheme 3).

In order to further understand the reaction mechanism, we
carried out a series of controlled laboratory experiments. First,
under the condition of acetone-d6 as the solvent, we observed
a deuterium incorporation rate of 13% in the product (Scheme
4, eq 1). This might be due to the acidic nature of the α-CH of
acetone, which could lead to the protonation of Co-allenyl inter-
mediates. In addition, we found that the initiation of the reaction
still requires the participation of DIPEA, verifying the importance

of amines (Scheme 4, eq 2). With CD OD as an additive, we
also observed a deuterium incorporation rate of 37%, indicating
that alcohol compounds act as protonolysis shuttle agents in the
reaction (Scheme 4, eq 3). However, due to the in-situ generation
of <sup>t</sup>BuOH in our system, the deuterium incorporation rate of the
product was not as high as in previous report.<sup>[9]</sup> Moreover, the
reaction was completely inhibited in the presence of the radical
scavenger 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinyloxy (TEMPO), which fully

demonstrated that the reaction involves a free radical process
(eq 4). At the same time, a product 3 captured by TEMPO was
identified by GC-MS, indicating that the DIPEA in the reaction
would form an alkyl radical under photocatalysis. Then, we per-
formed Stern-Volmer fluorescence quenching experiments and
showed that the photoexcited state of the photocatalyst was
eficiently quenched by DIPEA (Scheme 4, eq 4).

Based on the obtained results and previous reports,<sup>[9]</sup>
we speculate on the mechanism of the Co-catalyzed reduc-
tion of propargyl alcohol derivatives that we have developed
(Scheme 5). First, under the action of a photocatalyst, the

transformation from Co(II) to active Co(I) catalyst is achieved,
accompanied by the single-electron oxidation of DIPEA to
form intermediate A. The active Co(I) catalysis then under-
goes an

derivatives 1 to form an Co(III)-allenyl intermediate int-I
after releasing

Subsequently, under the action of
the alkyl radical specie B which generated from intermedi-

occurs to generate the Co(II)-allenyl intermediate int-II, which
is finally protonated to produce the allene products 2 and
<sup>t</sup>BuOCo(II).
3. Conclusion

In summary, a method for the photocatalytic reduction of
propargyl alcohols has been successfully developed, capable of
achieving an eficient transformation of a series of propargyl
alcohols into allene compounds, particularly the synthesis of
1,3-diarylallenes. This method has several advantages, including
good yields, good functional group tolerance, the use of the
inexpensive metal cobalt as a catalyst without the need for addi-
tional ligands, the use of organic amines as a hydrogen source
without the need for hydride additives, and the use of non-toxic
solvents. More transformations of propargyl alcohol derivatives
catalyzed by cobalt are under development in our lab.
